scenes.tts: The first film followed atoms through connected cycles. What happens when people make one flow much larger than before? Return to the same watershed and watch the amounts change.
scenes.caption: The first film followed atoms through connected cycles. What happens when people make one flow much larger than before? Return to the same watershed and watch the amounts change.
scenes.visual: Hook before title. Rebuild the first film's schematic farm, river, Bay, sky, crab, and underground layer in the same positions. COLOR MAP reused exactly: water blue, carbon orange, nitrogen green, sunlight gold, human-added flow red outline only. A red outline pulses around one incoming arrow without changing its concept color.
scenes.narration: The first film followed atoms through connected cycles. What happens when people make one flow much larger than before? Return to the same watershed and watch the amounts change.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the same dimmed watershed. Keep tokens moving behind the letters.

scenes.tts: A flow is matter moving between reservoirs during some time. Picture each reservoir with an amount meter. Arrows show matter entering or leaving. Their widths show relative flow, and every amount here is schematic.
scenes.caption: A flow is matter moving between reservoirs during some time. Picture each reservoir with an amount meter. Arrows show matter entering or leaving. Their widths show relative flow, and every amount here is schematic.
scenes.visual: Beside the carried landscape, add a large transparent reservoir tank with a vertical AMOUNT meter. Grow one arrow in and one arrow out. Change each arrow's width as tokens move. Keep a permanent 'schematic' label beside the tank.
scenes.narration: A flow is matter moving between reservoirs during some time. Picture each reservoir with an amount meter. Arrows show matter entering or leaving. Their widths show relative flow, and every amount here is schematic.

scenes.tts: If matter enters and leaves at matching rates, the amount can stay steady. That does not mean atoms stop. Tokens keep crossing both boundaries while the meter remains level.
scenes.caption: If matter enters and leaves at matching rates, the amount can stay steady. That does not mean atoms stop. Tokens keep crossing both boundaries while the meter remains level.
scenes.visual: Match the widths of the incoming and outgoing arrows. Send equal streams of tokens through the tank while its amount meter holds level. Add a small label, SAME AMOUNT, then keep both streams moving to show that steady is not stopped.
scenes.narration: If matter enters and leaves at matching rates, the amount can stay steady. That does not mean atoms stop. Tokens keep crossing both boundaries while the meter remains level.

scenes.tts: Coal, oil, and natural gas hold carbon that was underground for millions of years. Combustion moves that old carbon into today's air quickly. Plants and the ocean take up some added carbon, but combustion adds it faster than they remove it.
scenes.caption: Coal, oil, and natural gas hold carbon that was underground for millions of years. Combustion moves that old carbon into today's air quickly. Plants and the ocean take up some added carbon, but combustion adds it faster than they remove it.
scenes.visual: Reveal a large underground reservoir labeled FOSSIL FUELS. Orange tokens rise through a COMBUSTION arrow into the air; outline this orange arrow in red to mark a human-added flow. Draw the large natural exchanges as faint two-way orange arrows between air, plants and ocean, labeled TWO-WAY EXCHANGE, never compared by width with the combustion arrow. Then add two thinner one-way orange arrows labeled NET UPTAKE: PLANTS and NET UPTAKE: OCEAN, narrower together than the combustion arrow, so the air reservoir's meter creeps upward. No values.
scenes.narration: Coal, oil, and natural gas hold carbon that was underground for millions of years. Combustion moves that old carbon into today's air quickly. Plants and the ocean take up some added carbon, but combustion adds it faster than they remove it.

scenes.tts: Start from the balanced tank. Now the incoming flow grows wider, while the outgoing flow stays the same. What happens to the amount in the reservoir? Hold your answer.
scenes.caption: Start from the balanced tank. Now the incoming flow grows wider, while the outgoing flow stays the same. What happens to the amount in the reservoir? Hold your answer.
scenes.visual: Return to the large schematic tank from the balance scene, with matched arrows and a level meter. Widen only the incoming arrow. Keep the outgoing arrow unchanged. Freeze the amount meter before it responds, display the question, and let tokens continue approaching the boundary.
scenes.narration: Start from the balanced tank. Now the incoming flow grows wider, while the outgoing flow stays the same. What happens to the amount in the reservoir? Hold your answer.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep the widened incoming arrow, unchanged outgoing arrow, and question visible. Tokens drift toward the tank, but the amount meter still waits.

scenes.tts: The amount rises, because now more matter enters than leaves. The atoms were not created. They moved from another reservoir, and the receiving reservoir gained them.
scenes.caption: The amount rises, because now more matter enters than leaves. The atoms were not created. They moved from another reservoir, and the receiving reservoir gained them.
scenes.visual: Release the waiting tokens into the tank and raise the amount meter smoothly. Draw a dotted line back to a shrinking source tank, so the picture shows transfer rather than creation. Keep both tanks and all arrows marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: The amount rises, because now more matter enters than leaves. The atoms were not created. They moved from another reservoir, and the receiving reservoir gained them.

scenes.tts: People also add usable nitrogen to fields as fertilizer. Rain and flowing water can carry some nitrogen toward streams and the Bay. This human-added flow rides inside the water cycle.
scenes.caption: People also add usable nitrogen to fields as fertilizer. Rain and flowing water can carry some nitrogen toward streams and the Bay. This human-added flow rides inside the water cycle.
scenes.visual: Restore the watershed. Add green fertilizer tokens to the field with a red outline marking the addition. Blue rain falls. Blue runoff encloses some green tokens and carries them into the river, while other green tokens remain in soil. Never show all fertilizer leaving.
scenes.narration: People also add usable nitrogen to fields as fertilizer. Rain and flowing water can carry some nitrogen toward streams and the Bay. This human-added flow rides inside the water cycle.

scenes.tts: Not every added nitrogen atom takes the same route. Some stays on land, some enters living things, some reaches water, and some returns to the air as gas. The important question is how the added flow changes each reservoir over time.
scenes.caption: Not every added nitrogen atom takes the same route. Some stays on land, some enters living things, some reaches water, and some returns to the air as gas. The important question is how the added flow changes each reservoir over time.
scenes.visual: Split the newly added green tokens along four clearly labeled possible paths: STAYS ON LAND, LIVING THINGS, WATER, and AIR. Use dotted branch arrows and the word 'some' on each branch. Slowly update four schematic amount meters without showing exact values.
scenes.narration: Not every added nitrogen atom takes the same route. Some stays on land, some enters living things, some reaches water, and some returns to the air as gas. The important question is how the added flow changes each reservoir over time.

scenes.tts: How can scientists tell whether a cycle changed? A measurement records something observed, such as carbon dioxide in sampled air. A model combines observations and assumptions to estimate flows that cannot all be measured directly.
scenes.caption: How can scientists tell whether a cycle changed? A measurement records something observed, such as carbon dioxide in sampled air. A model combines observations and assumptions to estimate flows that cannot all be measured directly.
scenes.visual: Split the frame without leaving the watershed. Over the sky, an air-sampling instrument sends orange points to a blank trend axis labeled MEASURED RECORD. Over the watershed, map layers stack into a computer block and send green arrows to a label, MODELED FLOWS. Do not plot lesson values.
scenes.narration: How can scientists tell whether a cycle changed? A measurement records something observed, such as carbon dioxide in sampled air. A model combines observations and assumptions to estimate flows that cannot all be measured directly.

scenes.tts: Each kind of evidence has limits. One station is not the whole atmosphere. A watershed model estimates rather than measures every stream. Its result also depends on which sources the model includes.
scenes.caption: Each kind of evidence has limits. One station is not the whole atmosphere. A watershed model estimates rather than measures every stream. Its result also depends on which sources the model includes.
scenes.visual: Zoom out from the sampling instrument to a globe outline and label ONE STATION. Then zoom from the model block to several tributaries, some solid and some dotted, labeled ESTIMATES. Slide a visible boundary around a subset of source icons to show that inclusion matters.
scenes.narration: Each kind of evidence has limits. One station is not the whole atmosphere. A watershed model estimates rather than measures every stream. Its result also depends on which sources the model includes.

scenes.tts: Use each source for the question it can answer. A measured record shows what changed at its sampling place. A model can compare estimated sources across a watershed, if its boundaries and assumptions stay clear.
scenes.caption: Use each source for the question it can answer. A measured record shows what changed at its sampling place. A model can compare estimated sources across a watershed, if its boundaries and assumptions stay clear.
scenes.visual: Place the MEASURED RECORD and MODELED FLOWS cards side by side. Under the first, highlight SAMPLING PLACE. Under the second, highlight COMPARE SOURCES. Add visible tabs labeled BOUNDARIES and ASSUMPTIONS, then connect both cards to a large EVIDENCE label.
scenes.narration: Use each source for the question it can answer. A measured record shows what changed at its sampling place. A model can compare estimated sources across a watershed, if its boundaries and assumptions stay clear.

scenes.tts: Carbon and nitrogen follow different processes, yet the same reasoning applies. Identify the reservoir, compare what enters with what leaves, and ask which process changed the flow.
scenes.caption: Carbon and nitrogen follow different processes, yet the same reasoning applies. Identify the reservoir, compare what enters with what leaves, and ask which process changed the flow.
scenes.visual: Place an orange AIR reservoir and a green BAY WATER reservoir side by side. Show FIELD RUNOFF as a green input arrow into BAY WATER, not as a reservoir. Animate separate concept-colored flows around each. Under both, build the same tracker: RESERVOIR, IN VERSUS OUT, CHANGED PROCESS. Keep all arrows moving.
scenes.narration: Carbon and nitrogen follow different processes, yet the same reasoning applies. Identify the reservoir, compare what enters with what leaves, and ask which process changed the flow.

scenes.tts: When more matter enters a reservoir than leaves it, the amount rises. The next step is evidence: compare measured records with modeled flows, then keep their different limits in view.
scenes.caption: When more matter enters a reservoir than leaves it, the amount rises. The next step is evidence: compare measured records with modeled flows, then keep their different limits in view.
scenes.visual: Bring the carried watershed back to full frame. Widen one orange input and one green input at separate times, while their outgoing arrows stay the same; their reservoir meters rise. Then settle on two large evidence cards, MEASURED and MODELED, each with a small LIMITS tab.
scenes.narration: When more matter enters a reservoir than leaves it, the amount rises. The next step is evidence: compare measured records with modeled flows, then keep their different limits in view.

scenes.visual: One-line end card only over the darkened watershed with gently moving tokens: 'When more matter enters a reservoir than leaves it, the amount rises.'
